name: GTK
summary: A cross-platform widget toolkit built on GObject types, event controllers, widget composition, and GDK display/surface backends for native application interfaces.

features.name: GObject-backed widget type system
features.description: GTK widgets and related objects use GObject-derived types with class and instance structures, properties, signals, and reference-counted lifecycle conventions. GTK's public type declarations expose inheritance and interfaces while GObject supplies runtime type metadata.
benefits: Provides introspectable types, properties, and signals for language bindings
Supports reusable widget classes and interfaces
costs: Reference counting, disposal, and ownership conventions must be followed
Runtime type metadata increases framework surface area

features.name: Controller-based event dispatch
features.description: GTK attaches GtkEventController instances to widgets to receive and interpret input such as key, pointer, focus, motion, and scroll events. GDK event sources feed the toolkit while controllers provide phase, propagation, and gesture-specific handling.
benefits: Separates input recognition from widget implementation
Allows multiple controllers and propagation policies on a widget tree
costs: Propagation phases and controller ordering affect behavior

features.name: Hierarchical widget composition
features.description: GtkWidget exposes parent and child relationships and participates in allocation, measurement, focus, rendering, and state propagation. Composite widgets build application interfaces by nesting widgets under a root or application window.
benefits: Expresses UI containment and layout as a compositional tree
Enables inherited state, focus navigation, and coordinated rendering
costs: Tree mutation and layout invalidation create ordering and performance work
Widget lifecycle and parentage constrain reuse

features.name: GDK display and surface backend
features.description: GTK uses GDK display and surface abstractions for connection to window systems and input/rendering backends. The source tree contains backend-specific implementations for Wayland, X11, macOS, Windows, Android, and Broadway behind shared GDK interfaces.
benefits: Keeps widget code above native display-system details
Allows one toolkit API to target multiple window-system backends
costs: Backend capabilities and event semantics differ
Native integration and rendering behavior require platform-specific testing

mathematical_views.question: How do parent-child widget edges determine layout, focus, rendering, and lifecycle propagation?
assumptions: Widgets are nodes with typed properties and lifecycle state
Parent-child edges represent containment rather than ownership in every case
The model abstracts CSS/theme and renderer internals

mathematical_views.question: How do GDK events enter GTK and transition through event controllers and widget propagation phases?
assumptions: Input events have types and target surfaces/widgets
Controllers implement handling transitions and propagation policies

mathematical_views.question: Which common display, surface, and input operations are refined by a selected GDK backend?
assumptions: Equivalent behavior must be validated per backend and operation

benefits: Reusable and introspectable UI object contracts
costs: Dynamic type and ownership conventions increase lifecycle complexity

benefits: Input behavior can be composed independently of widgets
costs: Propagation and controller ordering can be difficult to reason about

benefits: UI structure and inherited behavior are explicit in a tree
costs: Layout invalidation and tree lifecycle add runtime work

benefits: Shared GTK APIs across multiple window systems
costs: Backend-specific capability and event differences remain
